Saryu Money: The Nirmaan Autopay Decision

Bengaluru, 15 September 2026

1. Opening

Rohit Bhargava reached his desk on the fourth floor of Saryu Money's Indiranagar office a little after eight, before the air conditioning had caught up with the Bengaluru morning. On his screen was a calendar invite for Friday, 18 September, three days away: "Product Council – Nirmaan Autopay Go/No-Go." He was the senior product manager for Collections and Credit, and the recommendation he carried into that room would decide whether Saryu Money switched on automatic UPI debit for eighteen hundred hardware and paint retailers who had never used the company's product before. Sales had already told the client it would happen by the first of October. The data scientist in Toronto had sent him a model he had not fully digested. The customer-success lead in Singapore had sent him a complaint log he wished he could unsee. He had three days to decide what to recommend, and to whom he owed the clearest explanation.

2. Company background

Saryu Money was a three-year-old Bengaluru fintech that lent working capital to small retailers — kirana stores, pharmacies, hardware shops — using cash-flow data pulled through India's Account Aggregator framework rather than collateral or a credit-bureau score alone. It disbursed through a partner non-banking financial company, priced its loans transparently in line with the Reserve Bank of India's 2022 digital lending guidelines, and repaid itself through UPI, the payments rail run by the National Payments Corporation of India. By the first quarter of FY27 it had lent a cumulative ₹640 crore to 46,000 retailers across Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, with a Series C balance sheet that investors were now pushing hard toward profitability. It competed for the same merchants that PhonePe and Paytm courted through their lending marketplaces, and that Razorpay Capital chased from the online-first end of the market; Saryu Money's edge was that its underwriting and its collections both understood the rhythm of a small-town shop far better than a metro-built product could. That edge was precisely what was now being tested.

3. The situation

In August, after an eleven-month sales cycle, Saryu Money signed a letter of intent with Al Noor Retail Holdings, a Dubai-based trading house that owned Nirmaan Hardware & Paints, a chain of 1,800 franchisee-run stores across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar and a regional distributor for Asian Paints and several hardware brands. Al Noor wanted an ₹85 crore working-capital facility extended to its franchisees, and it was willing to backstop ten per cent of losses itself — but only if every EMI was collected by automatic UPI Autopay mandate, debited from each store's account on the fifth of the month, rather than the manual reminder-and-pay flow Saryu Money used elsewhere. Karthik Subramaniam, Saryu Money's sales head, working out of New Jersey to cover both the Gulf relationship and the US investor calls, had promised Al Noor's chief financial officer a live pilot within thirty days of signing; his FY27 number leaned on this single account more than any other in his book.

The trouble was in the details Karthik had not fully seen. Neha Kulkarni, the data scientist in Toronto who had modelled Nirmaan's franchisees against Saryu Money's existing base, found their average cash buffer was ₹18,000 against ₹52,000 for merchants already comfortable with autopay — and Nirmaan stores kept far more irregular sales calendars, tied to when paint and cement moved rather than a steady daily till. Sunita Rao, the customer-success lead based in Singapore, had run a smaller autopay pilot with 400 Punjab retailers that February and March; 5.5 per cent had dropped out after bounced mandates triggered ₹500 penalty charges that landed before month-end collections cleared. And Lukas Weber, the designer in Berlin who owned the consent screen, had flagged that the pilot's mandate-signing flow never clearly told a retailer the debit date could shift, which he worried sat uneasily against both the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's informed-consent standard and NPCI's own requirement that a customer receive notice at least twenty-four hours before an automatic debit. The engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, who had built the pilot's Autopay integration, told Rohit plainly that the pre-debit notification workflow was only seventy per cent complete and would need three more weeks to meet that twenty-four-hour standard at scale.

4. The people

Faisal Al Mansoori — Chief Financial Officer, Al Noor Retail Holdings, Dubai. He is underwriting ten per cent of first losses on the ₹85 crore facility and wants Autopay live on the first of October precisely because it converts an uncertain manual collection into a guaranteed monthly debit; without it, he has said, he cannot justify the guarantee to his own board.
Karthik Subramaniam — Sales Head, based in New Jersey. He closed the largest single account of his tenure and has told Faisal it will be live in thirty days; a delay costs him credibility with the client and with Saryu Money's own leadership ahead of his FY27 target review.
Neha Kulkarni — Data Scientist, Toronto. Her risk model gates the launch; she wants the rollout sized to what the evidence supports, not to the sales timeline, and has asked to see thirty days of real repayment data from any new cohort before it scales.
Sunita Rao — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. She owns the retailer relationship after launch and carries the scar tissue of the Punjab pilot; she wants any rollout to fix the notification gap first, or she predicts a repeat at four and a half times the scale.

6. The options

Option A — Launch Autopay to all 1,800 stores by 1 October, as promised.

This keeps Karthik's word to Faisal, protects the ₹85 crore facility outright, and lets Rohit report a client win to the Product Council. Its cost is that it launches before the pre-debit notification workflow is finished, at four and a half times the scale of a pilot that already produced a 5.5 per cent drop-out rate among retailers with thinner cash buffers than Saryu Money has ever collected from automatically. It exposes the company to a compliance gap on RBI's digital lending norms precisely where Nirmaan's own cash discipline is weakest.

Option B — Phase the rollout: 300 stores first, full scale by mid-November.

Rohit opens Autopay first to the 300 largest, longest-tenured Nirmaan stores, finishes the notification workflow over three weeks, and watches bounce and drop-out rates for thirty days before extending to the remaining 1,500. This answers Neha's evidence requirement and Sunita's notification fix directly, and it still delivers Faisal a live, working product — just not at full scale on his original date. The cost is the six-week gap in Exhibit 3, an estimated ₹60 lakh in deferred fees, and an uncomfortable call for Karthik to make to Dubai.

Option C — Decline Autopay for this segment; offer manual collection instead.

Rohit tells Al Noor that Nirmaan's franchisees will be served through Saryu Money's existing manual reminder-and-pay flow, with a dedicated relationship manager and WhatsApp nudges, not automatic debit. This removes the consent and compliance risk entirely and protects retailer trust without qualification. Its cost is that Faisal's first-loss guarantee was explicitly conditioned on Autopay; without it, Al Noor may walk to a lender who will offer it, and Saryu Money likely loses the facility altogether.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, map each stakeholder by power and interest. Which stakeholder's needs must be satisfied before the launch can proceed at all, and which can be managed through communication rather than through changing the product?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 say about the specific risk Autopay poses to Nirmaan's franchisees, as distinct from the risk Saryu Money already carries with its existing base? Whose evidence in the case speaks most directly to that risk?
  3. For each of Rohit's three options, identify who gains power, who loses power, and who is exposed to a risk they did not choose. Does any option change what the "sleeping" stakeholder in Exhibit 1 — the regulator — is likely to do next?
  4. Which option should Rohit recommend to the Product Council on 18 September, and what should Karthik say to Faisal Al Mansoori if it is not full-scale launch on 1 October?

8. A note for the learner

Stakeholder mapping earns its place in this case because the loudest voices — the client and the sales head, both high power and highly engaged — are not the only ones who can stop this launch. Exhibit 1 places the regulator in the upper-left quadrant: high power, low visible interest. It is not writing memos or joining calls, but its rules on pre-debit notice and informed consent will still apply the day something goes wrong, and by then the cost is no longer ₹60 lakh in deferred fees but a regulatory examination of Saryu Money's entire digital lending practice. A stakeholder map that only tracks who is asking loudest for something will miss exactly this actor, and this is the trap the case is built to expose: reading Exhibit 1 correctly means treating Neha's and Sunita's evidence not as friction to be managed around, but as the information that keeps the sleeping stakeholder asleep.

A well-reasoned answer identifies each stakeholder's power and interest before choosing an option, ties the choice explicitly to the evidence in Exhibit 2, and states plainly what is being given up. On that basis, Option B is the most defensible path. It satisfies Faisal's core interest — a working, live product with his guarantee in force — without launching before the notification workflow is compliant, and it uses Neha's and Sunita's evidence rather than overriding it. It costs Karthik an uncomfortable conversation and Rohit six weeks he would rather not spend, but both costs are visible, bounded and recoverable. Option A trades a known, moderate delay cost for an unbounded tail risk sized by exactly the population — thin-buffer, irregular-cash retailers — least able to absorb it. Option C is the safest reading of the regulator's interest but assumes, without testing it, that a narrower and better-built version of Autopay could not have kept the client at all; it gives away the facility before the case for keeping it responsibly has been tried.

Stakeholder mapping and management

Who decides, who influences, who blocks — and why the second question is the one that determines whether your decision survives the quarter.

Section oneTwo decisions, two weeks apart

On 6 January 2026, Ira Chaturvedi chaired a review that lasted four hours and produced no decision. She is vice-president of product at Phalguni Health Systems, a Pune company whose hospital information system runs the clinical and billing workflows of 240 hospital sites across fourteen Indian states, representing ₹210 crore of licence and subscription revenue and a further ₹44 crore of implementation and configuration services. The question on the table had been live for eleven months: whether to deprecate Site Forms, the customisation layer that lets each hospital rewrite screens, validation rules and clinical order sets to taste, and move every customer to a standard configuration model by 1 April 2026.

The engineering argument was not seriously contested. Site Forms had produced 3,100 distinct form variants across 240 sites; a single change to the discharge-summary schema, required to stay aligned with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's health-record specifications, had to be regression-tested against 3,100 variants and took, by measurement, nineteen engineer-weeks. Standardisation would cut that to eleven engineer-days. What was contested was everything else. Fifty-eight per cent of Phalguni's ₹44 crore services revenue was Site Forms work, and Yashwant Kelkar, the senior vice-president of professional services, had said in November that deprecation would "remove the reason customers renew with our people rather than a systems integrator." Meanwhile Dr Nandita Rane, chief medical information officer at Mangalvan Hospitals — twenty-eight hospitals, ₹19 crore of annual contract value, and the chair of Phalguni's twelve-member customer clinical council — had circulated a two-page note arguing that standard order sets were a patient-safety regression at hospitals with unusual case mixes. Dr Rane is not an employee of Phalguni. She has no vote, no seat on any committee inside the company, and no line in the programme's governance document. Ira had come to believe she was the most important person in the decision.

Nine hundred kilometres north, on 19 January, Varun Sathe was working the same problem in an entirely different shape. He is director of product at Mandaar Freight Exchange, a Gurugram marketplace that matches shippers with fleet owners across long-haul road lanes: 2,100 active shippers, 6,800 active fleet owners averaging 4.2 trucks each, ₹1,840 crore of annualised booking value and a 4.1 per cent take rate, or ₹75.4 crore of revenue. Mandaar wanted to make payment escrow mandatory from 1 February: shipper funds would be held for forty-eight hours after proof of delivery rather than released on delivery confirmation, so that damage and short-delivery disputes could be adjudicated before money moved.

Shippers wanted it badly. Fleet owners, who are small businesses running on borrowed working capital, read it as the platform taking custody of their cash. The arithmetic of the actual harm was almost comically small: on an average settlement of ₹86,000 per trip and eleven trips a month, a four-truck owner turns over ₹9.46 lakh a month, and two extra days of float at an eighteen per cent annual borrowing rate costs ₹933. The arithmetic of the political harm was not small at all. And Varun's problem, like Ira's, was that the people who would decide — Mandaar's executive committee — were not the people who could stop it. The people who could stop it were 6,800 fleet owners who talk to each other constantly on messaging groups organised by lane, and forty-one regional operations managers inside Mandaar whose variable pay is calculated on active-supply counts.

Both of these are stakeholder problems, and both of them are the version of the stakeholder problem that the standard treatment handles badly. The standard treatment scores people on power and interest and tells you to manage the high-high quadrant closely. It is not wrong. It is merely insufficient, in a specific and diagnosable way: it treats power as an attribute of a person, when the evidence from both of these situations is that power is a property of a position in a network of relationships and a structure of resource dependence. The argument of this page is that the whole practice becomes tractable once you take that seriously — and that the places where competent practitioners disagree are precisely the places where they have taken it seriously in different ways.

Section twoThe idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

A stakeholder is any party who can affect the outcome of a decision or is materially affected by it. The word was coined in a 1963 internal memorandum at the Stanford Research Institute as a deliberate pun on stockholder — "those groups without whose support the organization would cease to exist" — and entered management thought properly with R. Edward Freeman's Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach in 1984. Stakeholder mapping is the enumeration and classification of those parties for a named decision; stakeholder management is the allocation of finite attention across them and the choice of what evidence to give each.

The intellectual history has four strands worth separating, because practitioners today still argue along the seams between them.

The attribute strand begins with Aubrey Mendelow's power–interest grid in 1981 and reaches its most careful form in Ronald Mitchell, Bradley Agle and Donna Wood's 1997 paper in the Academy of Management Review, which argues that a claimant becomes salient to a manager in proportion to how many of three attributes they hold: power (capacity to impose their will), legitimacy (a socially accepted claim) and urgency (time-sensitivity). Their typology of eight classes — dormant, discretionary, demanding, dominant, dangerous, dependent, definitive — is a genuinely useful vocabulary, and its most valuable entry is the dangerous stakeholder: power and urgency without legitimacy, which is the profile of a stakeholder who will act coercively because no legitimate channel exists for them.

The structural strand begins with Jeffrey Pfeffer and Gerald Salancik's The External Control of Organizations (1978), whose resource-dependence theory holds that power accrues to whoever controls a resource that is critical, scarce and not substitutable — and therefore that power is a property of a dependency, not a person. Timothy Rowley's 1997 paper pushed this further into network terms: influence depends on the density of ties among stakeholders and on the focal firm's centrality within them. Two people with identical power and interest scores have materially different influence if one of them chairs a council of twelve and the other does not.

The decision-rights strand is practitioner-led and largely indifferent to mapping. It runs from Richard Beckhard and Reuben Harris's responsibility charting in the 1970s through RACI and its descendants — DACI, popularised at Intuit, with its explicit separation of Driver from Approver — to Andy Grove's treatment in High Output Management (1983) of position power versus knowledge power in dual-reporting organisations, and to the single-threaded-owner model that Amazon made famous. Its claim is that alignment problems are ownership problems wearing a disguise, and that the durable remedy is a written allocation of rights enforced by a named tie-breaker.

The normative strand is Freeman's own later position, sharpened by Thomas Donaldson and Lee Preston's 1995 distinction between descriptive, instrumental and normative stakeholder theory. It holds that stakeholders have claims that are intrinsically worth considering, independent of their capacity to hurt you — and therefore that a map which allocates attention strictly in proportion to blocking power is not merely incomplete but ethically inverted.

These four are not a synthesis waiting to happen. Each would decline to sign a specific proposition the others accept. The attribute school will sign "a manager can rank claimants by scored attributes and allocate attention accordingly" and will not sign "a stakeholder's power cannot be assessed without knowing who else they talk to." The structural school signs the second and declines the first. The decision-rights school will sign "most alignment failures are ownership failures" and will not sign "informal influence mapping substitutes for a written decision record"; it regards a beautifully maintained influence map in an organisation with unclear ownership as an expensive symptom. The normative school will sign "a stakeholder with a legitimate claim and no power still deserves consideration" and will not sign the attention-allocation formula that sections three and eight of this page will develop. A fifth position exists and is held privately by many senior practitioners: that mapping is over-engineering, that what works is durable relationships built before they are needed, and that a product manager who is scoring a colleague on a five-point scale has already lost something that cannot be recovered by arithmetic.

Section threeMechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

What expert practitioners actually do has five moves. Three of them appear in every textbook. Two do not, and the two that do not are where the leverage is.

Move one: bound the decision until the list is finite

"Stakeholders of the platform team" is not a list. "People who can affect, or are affected by, the choice to deprecate Site Forms with a hard cutover on 1 April 2026" is a list of eight. The discipline is that no name enters without a one-clause statement of the mechanism by which it touches this choice. Maps of forty names are maps of a territory, and they are unusable because attention cannot be allocated across forty people; an expert reading such a map assumes it has never been used to make a decision.

Move two: separate decision rights from influence, and draw both

Decision rights are a matter of record — who is accountable, who is consulted, who holds a veto and on what specific grounds. Influence is a matter of observed behaviour — whose opinion moves the accountable person. The two pictures diverge in every organisation above roughly a hundred people, and the divergence is not a pathology to be corrected; it is the operating reality that the decision record exists to constrain. Ira's programme charter named her and the chief technology officer, Anita Sequeira, as joint deciders, with the head of regulatory affairs, Meera Joshi, holding a veto on data-specification grounds. That document is accurate and it does not predict the outcome.

Move three: score attributes — and then correct them for network position

This is the first of the two moves that textbooks skip. Score raw power P on one to five, where the justification must name a mechanism rather than a feeling. Then estimate, for each ordered pair, a weight wij in the range zero to one: how much does person j weight person i's view on a question of this kind? Effective power is then raw power plus a discounted sum of the power of the people you move:

Ei = Pi + α · Σj ( wij · Pj ), with α set to 0.5 for one step of propagation

The choice of α is a judgement about how lossy influence is; 0.5 says that moving someone who can move a five is worth about as much as being a two-and-a-half yourself. The absolute numbers do not matter. What matters is the ratio Ai = Ei / Pi, the amplification factor, which identifies the people whose apparent standing understates their reach. That ratio is the single most useful number the practice produces, and it is invisible to a power–interest grid.

The computation for Dr Nandita Rane, node by node. She moves Girish Pathak, the western regional sales head, strongly — weight 0.8 — because Mangalvan is his largest reference account and its clinical council seat is the thing he sells with; Girish's raw power is 3, contributing 2.4. She moves the chief executive, Suchitra Balan, at weight 0.4, because Suchitra reads the clinical council's minutes personally; Suchitra's power is 5, contributing 2.0. And she moves the other eleven chief medical information officers on the council at weight 0.7, contributing 0.7 × 3 = 2.1. The sum is 6.5; at α = 0.5, her effective power is 3 + 3.25 = 6.25, against a raw score of 3 and a theoretical maximum raw score of 5. Her amplification factor is 2.08 — the highest in the network by a distance.

A power–interest grid would have placed her in the "keep informed" quadrant and a diligent programme manager would have sent her a monthly newsletter.

Move four: record required stance separately from current stance, and allocate to the gap

Most maps record only how supportive a person is. The operative quantity is the distance between where they stand and where they need to stand for the decision to survive. Score stance from −2 (would actively oppose) to +2 (would champion publicly). Salience S is effective power times interest. The gap is G = S × (R − C) where R is the required stance and C the current one, floored at zero, and engagement hours are allocated as hi = H · Gi / ΣGj.

Choosing R modestly is how a product manager buys back time, and it is a genuine decision rather than an observation. Ira set Dr Rane's required stance at 0, not +1: Mangalvan did not need to endorse deprecation, it needed to not organise against it. That single choice changed the conversation from persuasion to negotiation, which is a different activity with a different success criterion.

Move five: solve for the fixed point, because the allocation changes the inputs

This is the second skipped move and the most important second-order effect in the whole practice. Because stakeholders influence each other, moving one changes the stances of others, which changes their gaps, which changes the allocation. The naive procedure — score once, allocate once — treats a simultaneous system as if it were a list.

Ira ran it as two iterations. In the first pass, the total gap across her eight stakeholders was 118 units and Dr Rane's share entitled her to 3.4 of Ira's twelve weekly hours. Ira then asked a different question: if four hours a week moved Dr Rane from −2 to 0, what happens downstream? Girish Pathak's stance was −1 almost entirely because his reference account was unhappy; the model predicted he would move to 0 unaided, cutting his gap from 12 to 4. The clinical council's aggregate stance was −1 with weight 0.7 flowing from Dr Rane; its gap fell from 18 to 6. Total gap fell from 118 to 78 — but 40 of the 118 units had been retired by engagement with a single person who, on the raw grid, ranked joint last. The second iteration reallocated the freed 5.6 hours toward Yashwant Kelkar, whose opposition was structural rather than informational and whom no amount of talking to somebody else would move.

The lesson generalises. Gaps that are downstream of another stakeholder's stance are not independent claims on your time; they are symptoms. Identifying which gaps are symptoms and which are sources is the difference between a practitioner who is busy and one who is effective, and it falls directly out of the influence weights.

Section fourWhen the idea applies, and when it is actively misleading

The method rests on four conditions. Each can be stated as a testable claim, and each can be checked against both protagonists.

Condition one: the decision is discrete, dated and reversible-at-a-cost. Mapping allocates attention against a deadline; without one there is no basis for the allocation, and without a real reversal cost there is no reason to pay for alignment at all. Phalguni passes emphatically — 1 April 2026, and a reversal would be visible to every customer. Mandaar passes with a caveat: the escrow rule is technically reversible in a day, which tempts the team to treat alignment as optional, and it is exactly that temptation that produces the pattern of ship-then-retreat that erodes supply-side trust faster than the original change ever would have.

Condition two: the set of consequential parties is enumerable. Phalguni's is: eight people, two of them external, all nameable. Mandaar's is not, and this is the single most important analytical fact about Varun's situation. Six thousand eight hundred fleet owners cannot be mapped. The available move is to map the structures through which they act — the lane-level messaging groups, the four regional fleet-owner associations, the nine largest operators who each run more than forty trucks and whose withdrawal would visibly thin specific lanes — and to accept that the map is of channels rather than of claimants. Practitioners who apply person-level mapping to a mass-market side of a marketplace produce documents that are precise and useless.

Condition three: stances are informative rather than performed. The model assumes that what someone tells you approximates what they will do. In organisations with low psychological safety, or where the product manager is perceived as carrying the chief executive's preference, stated stance is close to uncorrelated with behaviour, and the arithmetic then launders agreeableness into false confidence. The diagnostic is simple and uncomfortable: if nobody in your map is at −2 and at least one person is a loser under the proposed change, you are not measuring stance, you are measuring politeness.

Condition four: your attention is the scarce input. Sometimes it is not. Where the binding constraint is a budget, a regulatory calendar or an engineering dependency, stakeholder work has low marginal return and the honest answer is to spend less on it. The failure mode here has a name inside large companies — alignment theatre — and it is expensive precisely because it is indistinguishable from diligence.

There are three situations where mapping is not merely inapplicable but misleading. The first is a genuine emergency, where the map's implicit assumption that consent can be cultivated over weeks is false and the correct behaviour is to act and account for it afterwards. The second is a decision that is properly somebody else's: mapping a decision you do not own converts a clean escalation into a shadow campaign, and the tell is a map in which the accountable person appears as a target rather than as the decider. The third is any situation where the legitimate claimants are systematically powerless — patients whose records Phalguni holds, owner-drivers who are not the fleet owners Mandaar contracts with — because an attention-allocation formula keyed to blocking power will reliably rank them last, and the formula's silence on this is not a gap in the data but a property of the objective function.

Section fiveHard edge cases and the organisational seams

Two-sided markets: the stakeholders are structurally opposed

In a marketplace the two sides are not two customer segments; they are parties whose interests are genuinely, not apparently, in tension, because most changes redistribute value between them. Mandaar's escrow proposal is a transfer: shippers gain dispute protection worth, by Varun's estimate, ₹4.6 crore a year in avoided write-offs and reduced churn; fleet owners lose ₹933 a month each in float cost, which across 6,800 owners is ₹7.6 crore a year in aggregate — a transfer that is negative-sum in raw rupees and was justified internally on the grounds that it would raise shipper retention.

The seam at the foot of Figure 2 is the general case, not a Mandaar peculiarity. Wherever two functions are measured on quantities that the same change moves in opposite directions, their stances are determined before the discussion begins, and treating them as opinions to be shifted by evidence is a category error. The expert move is to go after the measurement rather than the stance: Varun's eventual proposal included a three-month adjustment to the regional managers' supply-count target, which cost ₹38 lakh in variable pay and did more for the decision's survival than any amount of explanation.

Regulated products: some stakeholders cannot be negotiated with

Phalguni operates inside a genuine regulatory frame — the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's health-data specifications, NABH accreditation requirements at customer hospitals, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — and the important property of a regulatory constraint is that it is not a stakeholder with a stance. It is a boundary condition. The common and costly confusion is to place the internal regulatory-affairs function on the map at a stance of −1 and set about moving it, when what the function is doing is reporting a constraint. The diagnostic is to ask the regulatory lead a single question: "Is this your judgement or your reading of the requirement?" An expert asks it early, because the two answers demand completely different responses, and a regulatory function that is repeatedly treated as an opponent stops distinguishing between them out of self-protection.

Hardware plus software: the map acquires a time axis

Mausam Grid Systems, an Ahmedabad manufacturer of solar inverters sold with a monitoring application, illustrates a property that pure-software practitioners rarely internalise. A stakeholder's stance can only be revised while the decision is still open to them, and in hardware most of them close early. Mausam's contract manufacturer requires a bill-of-materials freeze sixteen weeks before shipment; a change requiring safety re-certification costs ₹34 lakh and nine weeks; channel distributors commit inventory six weeks out; installers are trained three weeks out; the companion app can change the night before. Ordering stakeholder engagement by power produces the wrong sequence. Ordering it by last responsible moment produces the right one.

AI-native products: three stakeholders that did not exist before

Mukhaatib AI, a Bengaluru company whose conversational agent handles first-line claims queries for insurers including Manjari Insurance Services, has a stakeholder map with three entries that would have been unintelligible a decade ago. The first is the customer's internal audit function, which must now form a view about a system whose outputs are non-deterministic; the evidence it needs is not a specification but an evaluation set with coverage and confidence intervals, and product managers who send it a specification receive a delay they cannot diagnose. The second is Mukhaatib's own evaluation and labelling team: because their rubric defines what counts as a correct answer, they hold real decision rights over product behaviour that appear in no governance document, and the tell-tale sign is a rubric change that ships without review while a copy change requires three approvals. The third is the foundation-model vendor, which is a stakeholder with overwhelming power, zero interest in any individual customer's roadmap, and no negotiation surface at all: when a model version was scheduled for retirement with ninety days' notice, Mukhaatib absorbed roughly 600 engineer-hours of re-evaluation and had to re-open Manjari's audit sign-off, which had been granted against a version that would no longer exist. The correct treatment of such a party is not engagement. It is contingency: the map should carry, for each exogenous dependency, the cost and lead time of the response rather than a stance.

What mature companies actually do at the seams

The public account is that seams are resolved by clear ownership documents. The observable practice in most large Indian and global product organisations is different and worth stating plainly. Seams are resolved by a standing forum with a named tie-breaker who is one level above both functions, meeting on a fixed cadence, with an escalation service level — and where that forum does not exist, they are resolved by whichever executive has the chief executive's attention that quarter. Mature organisations are not ones where the second mechanism has been eliminated. They are ones where the first mechanism handles enough volume that the second is used rarely enough to remain cheap.

Section sixNine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Power is a property of a dependency, not of a person

Resource-dependence theory predicts that power follows control of a resource that is critical, scarce and hard to substitute. The practical consequence is that the same person scores differently on two decisions in the same quarter, and an expert is unsurprised by this. Tell-tale sign: a stakeholder map reused unchanged across two decisions. Why the obvious reading is wrong: it feels efficient, and it silently imports the power structure of the previous decision into a new one where the critical resource has changed hands.

The mixed-blessing stakeholder is the one to engage first

Savage, Nix, Whitehead and Blair proposed in 1991 that stakeholders be classified on two axes — potential for threat and potential for cooperation — producing a fourth type the power–interest grid cannot express: high on both. Yashwant Kelkar is exactly this. He can end the programme, and he is also the only person who can make the migration commercially survivable by running it as a paid service line. Tell-tale sign: the meeting you most dread. Why the obvious reading is wrong: the instinct is to build support elsewhere first and confront the mixed-blessing stakeholder from strength, which is precisely the sequence that converts a potential ally into a committed opponent.

Stated stance is measured with a systematic positive bias

People are more agreeable in one-to-one conversations with a colleague they like than in a room with their own team watching. The bias is not random noise; it is directional and it is largest for the people you talk to most. Tell-tale sign: unanimous private support followed by silence in the group review. Why the obvious reading is wrong: the silence is read as consent, when it is the first honest signal in the sequence. The expert correction is to collect at least one stance in a setting where the person's own constituency can hear them.

Legitimacy without power is the practice's structural blind spot

Patients whose records Phalguni processes, and owner-drivers who are employed by Mandaar's fleet owners rather than contracting with Mandaar, have unambiguous claims and no capacity to block anything. An attention formula keyed to gap and power will rank them last every time, and it will be arithmetically correct. Tell-tale sign: the people most affected by a decision appear nowhere on the map. Why the obvious reading is wrong: this is not a data-quality problem to be fixed by better enumeration; it is what the objective function is for, and the only remedy is an explicit second criterion applied outside the model.

Coalitions are not additive

Two stakeholders at −1 who have not spoken are two problems. The same two after a corridor conversation are one problem with a strategy, a shared vocabulary and roughly three times the effective power. Tell-tale sign: two people who do not normally work together begin using the same phrase — "patient-safety regression," in Phalguni's case, which appeared in Girish Pathak's pipeline review eight days after it appeared in Dr Rane's note. Why the obvious reading is wrong: the phrase sounds like independent corroboration and is in fact evidence of a single source.

Mapping is itself a political act

The document is an assessment of colleagues, written by someone with an interest in the outcome, and it does not stay private. Tell-tale sign: someone asks to see their own score. Why the obvious reading is wrong: the instinct is to conceal the map harder. The expert practice is to write every cell — particularly the "what they need" column — in language you would be content for its subject to read, which costs some analytical bluntness and buys a document that survives contact with the organisation.

A veto is not opposition and opposition is not a veto

A veto is a right to stop a decision on stated grounds; opposition is a preference. Conflating them inflates the apparent difficulty of a decision and, worse, teaches people that expressing displeasure functions as a veto — after which it does. Tell-tale sign: an escalation that produces a delay but never produces a decision. Why the obvious reading is wrong: the delay looks like due process and is actually an unowned veto being exercised by attrition.

Alignment is a stock that depreciates

Agreement obtained in November is not agreement held in February; people's own objectives have been reset in the interim and their memory of the reasoning has decayed. Tell-tale sign: you have to re-explain the same rationale to the same person twice in a quarter. Why the obvious reading is wrong: this is read as the person being difficult, when it is the ordinary depreciation rate of a commitment made against a context that has since changed. The remedy is a written decision record they can re-read, not a third conversation.

The map has an opportunity cost, and it is the product

Twelve hours a week of stakeholder work is twelve hours not spent with customers or in the problem. There exists a level of stakeholder management that is indistinguishable from not doing the job, and it is reached more often by strong practitioners than by weak ones, because they are good at it and it produces visible approval. Tell-tale sign: a product manager's calendar with no unbroken two-hour block in it. Why the obvious reading is wrong: a full calendar of alignment meetings reads as engagement and is frequently the leading indicator of a product that nobody is thinking about.

Section sevenVariation by product type and company stage

In consumer products the users are numerous and individually powerless, so the consequential stakeholders are overwhelmingly internal — brand, legal, trust and safety — plus a small number of exogenous powers with no negotiation surface: the app stores, the payment rails, and in India the regulatory calendar set by bodies such as the Reserve Bank of India for anything touching money movement. The characteristic failure is the high-power, low-interest general counsel who learns about a feature from a screenshot.

In B2B and enterprise the map crosses the company boundary as a matter of course, and it must be run twice: once inside your company and once inside the account, where the economic buyer, the technical approver, the daily user and the renewal signer are four people with conflicting interests. Phalguni's situation is the enterprise case in its purest form — an external clinician with no contractual standing outranking most of the executive team on effective power.

In platforms and marketplaces the defining feature is structural opposition between the sides and the impossibility of person-level mapping on the mass side. On platforms specifically, the developer ecosystem behaves like a supply side with an unusual property: its members' switching costs are sunk in code, which makes their stated stance far more stable than a marketplace participant's and their actual departure far more consequential when it happens.

In hardware and physical goods the time axis dominates, as Figure 3 shows, and a further asymmetry appears: some stakeholders — a contract manufacturer, a certification body — are not persuadable at all in the relevant window, so the map is partly a schedule of constraints rather than a plan of engagement.

In AI products the novelty is genuine but narrower than the discourse suggests. The mapping method is unchanged; what changes is that evaluation rubrics confer undocumented decision rights, that audit and risk functions require a new evidence type, and that model vendors are exogenous powers to be hedged rather than engaged. Where the difference is often claimed and is not real: AI does not make stakeholders more numerous or their interests less legible.

By stage, the honest account is that the difficulty is not monotonic. In a thirty-person company the map is unnecessary as a written artefact and the characteristic failure is a founder who is simultaneously decider, veto and loudest opinion, so that no stance in the room is independently measured. In a five-thousand-person company decision rights are documented, approvals are obtainable, and the binding problem is reversal — the map's value is almost entirely in the influence layer. The hardest stage is the middle, at roughly two hundred to eight hundred people, where the organisation has grown past the point where everyone knows everyone but has not yet written down who decides what. Both Phalguni, at 640 employees, and Mandaar, at 410, sit squarely in it.

Section eightThree worked examples, one of them a failure

Phalguni: pricing the reversal risk

Ira's central question about Yashwant Kelkar was not whether he was right but what his opposition cost in expectation. Phalguni had attempted four comparable platform-standardisation programmes since 2019; two had been reversed or indefinitely suspended within six months, and in both cases professional services had been at a negative stance at launch. Four observations is a thin base and Ira said so in writing, but it is the base that exists, and it implies a reversal probability of roughly 0.45 with Yashwant at −1.

The cost of a reversal she estimated at ₹8.4 crore: ₹3.1 crore of re-work to restore and re-certify the customisation layer, ₹4.0 crore of licence revenue deferred from the renewals that had been priced on the new model, and about 1,300 engineering hours valued at ₹1.3 crore. Expected cost of proceeding with Yashwant unmoved: 0.45 × 8.4 = ₹3.78 crore.

The cost of moving him she could also price, because the move was structural rather than rhetorical: transfer the migration programme to professional services as a chargeable service line, which required Phalguni to forgo ₹1.9 crore of product-side margin over four quarters. The comparison is 1.9 against 3.78, and the transfer is indicated. The breakeven reversal probability is 1.9 ÷ 8.4 = 0.226: below a 22.6 per cent chance of reversal, buying Yashwant's stance is not worth the margin.

It is that it converts an argument about whether Yashwant is being obstructive into an argument about a number, and the number it exposes — 22.6 per cent — is one that two reasonable people can disagree about productively. That is what a quantitative treatment of a political question is for.

Mandaar: the supply-side elasticity that decides the question

Varun's calculation ran the other way. The escrow's benefit to shippers was ₹4.6 crore a year. The relevant risk was not fleet-owner unhappiness in the abstract but lane coverage: Mandaar's fill-rate guarantee depends on at least three quotes per posted load, and 40 of its 310 lanes were already thin enough that a six per cent reduction in active fleet owners — 408 of 6,800 — would drop those lanes below the threshold. Below the threshold, shipper fill rate on those lanes falls from 94 to 88 per cent; the 40 thin lanes carry ₹214 crore of annual booking value, and a six-point fill-rate drop at a 4.1 per cent take rate is 214 × 0.06 × 0.041 = ₹5.3 lakh of direct revenue — trivially small, which is the trap. The shippers on those lanes are not lane-specific; they are national accounts that post on thin lanes and dense ones alike, and Varun's estimate was that a visible coverage failure on a thin lane puts roughly ₹31 crore of multi-lane booking value into renewal risk. The decision therefore hinges entirely on the supply-side elasticity, a number Mandaar did not have, and the correct first action was a two-week limited rollout on eleven lanes to measure it rather than any further stakeholder conversation.

Madhukosh Money: a textbook map that failed

Madhukosh Money, a Mumbai consumer savings application with 3.1 million registered users, provides the instructive failure. In June 2025 its product manager, Rhea Kamat, mapped nine stakeholders for a decision to auto-enrol existing users into a round-up savings feature, scored them carefully, and by late August had every one of them at +1 or better. The feature shipped on 4 September. It was suspended on 23 September, nineteen days later. Forty-one thousand users had to be un-enrolled, ₹2.7 crore of accumulated round-up balances reversed, and the direct cost in engineering and support came to ₹1.4 crore; the application's store rating fell from 4.4 to 4.0 over the following six weeks.

Three things had gone wrong, and none of them was carelessness. First, the map was of people rather than of institutions: the compliance officer scored at +2 left the company in July, and his successor read the same facts differently, as successors reliably do. Second, the map had no entry at all for the partner bank's product risk committee, which met monthly, had never been in any room Rhea was in, and held an effective veto on any change to how customer funds were swept. Third, every stance had been collected in a one-to-one conversation, where the positive bias described in section six is at its largest.

The recovery is the useful part. Madhukosh relaunched in February 2026 as an opt-in feature, taking a 22 per cent opt-in rate against the 100 per cent that auto-enrolment had produced on paper — a substantially worse headline number and a substantially better business, since the opted-in cohort's ninety-day retention was 71 per cent against the auto-enrolled cohort's 34 per cent. The structural fix was to replace the stakeholder list with an institutional register: the unit of analysis became the standing body or role — the partner bank's risk committee, the compliance function, the grievance officer under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act — with the current occupant recorded as an attribute of the row rather than as the row itself. Rhea's own summary, quoted in Madhukosh's internal review, was that she had mapped nine people accurately and the organisation she was actually operating in had seven institutions, four of which she had never named.

Section nineFailure modes, early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Mapping people rather than institutions. The early warning is a map whose rows are all individual names. The diagnostic question is: "If this person changed jobs tomorrow, does the row disappear or does it acquire a new occupant?" Caught early, the fix is a column. Caught late, it costs what Madhukosh paid — ₹1.4 crore and a rating.

Reading volume as power. The early warning is that the person who comments most in reviews also receives the most one-to-one time. The diagnostic question is: "Name the specific mechanism by which this person could stop this." If the answer is "they would be unhappy," it is not a mechanism. Caught late, the cost is not an incident but a quarter of misallocated attention, which is why it survives so long — it has no visible failure event.

Managing to consensus rather than to a sufficient stance. The early warning is a long alignment phase, a short build phase, and nobody visibly opposed. The diagnostic question is: "What is the minimum acceptable position for each person on this list?" If the answer is "supportive" for all of them, no prioritisation has happened. Caught late, the cost is a schedule: Phalguni's own eleven-month deliberation on a decision with nineteen engineer-weeks a year at stake is the example.

Engaging the top-right quadrant first. The early warning is that the high-power, low-interest stakeholders — risk, legal, regulatory, security — appear in the calendar last because they are not asking for meetings. The diagnostic question is: "Which constraint, if it exists, invalidates the date?" and it must be asked of those people specifically. Caught in month one it is a four-day change; caught in month six it is a five-week slip, and Phalguni's regulatory affairs function had exactly one such constraint waiting.

Treating the map as a private document. The early warning is a spreadsheet nobody outside the product manager has seen, usually because a cell would embarrass someone. The diagnostic question is: "Could the 'what they need' column be shown to the person it describes?" Caught late, the cost is the map's credibility and occasionally the product manager's, and it is not recoverable within the same programme.

Mistaking a boundary condition for a stance. The early warning is a regulatory or security colleague scored at −1 and an engagement plan aimed at moving them. The diagnostic question is the one in section five: "Is this your judgement or your reading of the requirement?" Caught late, the cost is worse than a delay — a compliance function that has learned to stop distinguishing between the two.

Failing to re-solve after an exogenous change. The early warning is a map with a date on it more than a month old, in a quarter when a target was reset. The diagnostic question is: "Whose objectives changed since this was written?" This one is cheap to catch and cheap to fix, and it is the most common of all.

Section tenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Position one: allocate attention in proportion to blocking power. In its strongest form this is not cynicism but an argument about consequences. A product manager has twelve hours a week; decisions that are reversed help nobody, least of all the powerless stakeholders in whose name the objection is raised; therefore the responsible act is to spend attention where it maximises the probability that a good decision survives. Its evidence is the reversal base rate — Phalguni's two-in-four — and the observation that organisations which do not manage blocking power do not thereby become more equitable, they merely become slower. It would be wrong if reversals were rare, or if attention spent on powerless stakeholders reliably produced better decisions rather than merely more legitimate ones.

Position two: the normative claim outranks the instrumental one. Stakeholders with legitimate claims and no power are exactly the parties whose interests markets fail to represent, and a profession that formalises their exclusion in a spreadsheet has made the failure durable and respectable. Its evidence is the pattern of consumer-product harms that were visible to the affected group long before they were visible to any powerful stakeholder. It would be wrong if the instrumental map and the normative one converged in practice — if attending to powerless claimants reliably paid for itself — and the honest reading of the evidence is that it sometimes does and sometimes does not.

Position three: the whole exercise is a symptom of missing decision rights. On this view, developed most sharply by practitioners from organisations with strong single-threaded ownership, a company that requires its product managers to run influence arithmetic has failed to write down who decides what, and every hour spent on the arithmetic is an hour spent maintaining the dysfunction. Its evidence is real: organisations that invested in explicit decision records report decision latency falling by large factors, and the alignment-theatre failure mode is unambiguous. It would be wrong if decision rights could not in fact be specified far enough in advance — and in genuinely novel decisions, which is most interesting ones, they frequently cannot, which is the strongest reply.

Position four: relationships, not maps. The senior practitioner's position is that a product manager who has had lunch with the compliance officer every quarter for two years does not need a gap score, because the constraint arrives in week one by telephone. Its evidence is the observed behaviour of the most effective people in most organisations, who do not maintain stakeholder spreadsheets. It would be wrong — and this is the reply its holders find hardest — in exactly the situations where it is most needed: a new joiner, a newly reorganised company, a decision that crosses into a function you have never worked with, or a marketplace where the stakeholder is six thousand people you will never meet. The strongest synthesis available is uncomfortable and not universally held: mapping is a technology for people who do not yet have the relationships, and its success condition is that it makes itself unnecessary.

Section elevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently from someone who has studied it in four observable ways. They begin with the decision rather than the people, and they can say in one sentence what is being decided and by whom, which sounds trivial and is the step most often skipped. They consult the high-power, low-interest parties first and the enthusiastic ones last, which inverts the natural order of who is easy to meet. They set required stances at the lowest level that works, so that most of their stakeholders require nothing at all, and they can tell you which of their open gaps are sources and which are symptoms of somebody else's stance. And they write the map in language its subjects could read, because they have concluded that the analytical honesty lost is smaller than the credibility gained.

There is a fifth mark, harder to observe and more diagnostic than the other four: they treat opposition as information before they treat it as an obstacle. Dr Rane's patient-safety objection was, on investigation, correct for nine of Mangalvan's twenty-eight hospitals and wrong for the other nineteen — a finding that changed Phalguni's product design and would never have surfaced from a plan aimed at moving her from −2 to 0.

Section twelveWhat each of them decided

Ira Chaturvedi recommended, on 3 February 2026, a modified deprecation. The 1 April cutover held for configuration and screen layout, where the 3,100 variants were largely cosmetic. Clinical order sets — the specific object of Dr Rane's objection — were carved out into a governed extension model with a published review process chaired by the clinical council, which converted Dr Rane from the decision's most dangerous opponent into the owner of its most sensitive component. The migration programme moved to professional services as a chargeable line at a cost of ₹1.9 crore in forgone product margin, justified by the Exhibit 2 arithmetic. Meera Joshi's record-retention constraint, surfaced on 14 January rather than in March, added four working days.

Varun Sathe did not decide. He converted the decision into a measurement: an eleven-lane limited rollout from 9 February, instrumented to estimate supply-side elasticity, with the forty-one regional managers' supply-count targets adjusted for the quarter at a cost of ₹38 lakh so that their measured incentive stopped contradicting the company's stated one. The escrow question remains open at Mandaar, which is the correct state for a question whose answer turns on a number nobody has.

Discussion questions.

1. Ira Chaturvedi's amplification analysis gave Dr Nandita Rane an effective power of 6.25 on a five-point scale. Is a model that produces out-of-range values telling you something real, or is it evidence that the underlying scale is mis-specified — and would the practical conclusion have changed if Ira had simply capped the scores at five?

2. Mandaar's regional managers were moved by changing their targets rather than their minds, at a cost of ₹38 lakh. Under what conditions is buying a stance through compensation design a legitimate instrument of product management, and under what conditions is it an admission that the organisation's incentive structure is doing the deciding?

3. Rhea Kamat's nine-person map was accurate and insufficient. If the unit of analysis should be institutions rather than people, what is lost — and how would a product manager detect that a named individual is about to deviate from what their institution would sanction?

Section thirteenGoing deeper

What a product manager does
The role is defined by the absence of authority over most of the people whose work must converge; stakeholders are simply the full list of those people, which is why this topic sits underneath almost everything else.
Prioritising under constraints
A stakeholder map produces a set of competing legitimate claims and no way to adjudicate between them; prioritisation supplies the adjudication, and reads badly without the map that generated the claims.
Communicating with leadership
The high-power, low-interest quadrant is largely made of executives; this topic is the specific craft of giving them the evidence type they need in the time they have.
Decision records and DACI/RACI
Turns the informal decision-rights picture into an artefact the organisation can be held to, and is the only durable defence against the reversal-by-attrition failure mode.
Status updates and stakeholder rhythms
Alignment depreciates; a cadence is how you pay the maintenance cost cheaply instead of re-persuading people from scratch each quarter.
Difficult conversations
The mixed-blessing stakeholder must be engaged early and directly; this topic is the technique for the conversation the map tells you to have first.
Listening and questioning
Stance scores are only as good as the elicitation; the positive-bias problem in section six is fundamentally a questioning problem.
Influence without authority
The map says who needs 3.4 hours a week; this topic addresses what actually happens inside them.
Working in diverse and global teams
Influence weights and the norms around expressing dissent vary sharply across offices and cultures, and a map calibrated in one and applied in another will be confidently wrong.
Working with data scientists and ML engineers
In AI products the evaluation rubric confers undocumented decision rights; this topic is how to work with the people who hold them.
Telling the customer story
The most portable currency across a stakeholder map, because it is the one form of evidence that travels between functions without losing its force.
Demo and pitch craft
For several stakeholder types a working demonstration is the evidence that moves them, and nothing else is.
Writing as a PM superpower
Maps, decision records and required-stance statements are all written artefacts; the quality of the writing determines whether they survive being forwarded.
Running effective meetings
Group settings are where stance is measured honestly; a badly run review destroys the only unbiased measurement you get.
Managing up and across
The operational discipline of maintaining relationships before they are needed, which is the position-four answer to the whole of this page.
Board and investor communication
The stakeholder set with the highest power, the lowest interest in detail and the longest memory for reversals — the quadrant where getting the sequence wrong is most expensive.

Aripan Systems: One Kohbar

Bengaluru, Sunday 8 November 2026

1. The night before

The power in Devika Ranjan's building on Sarjapur Road had been out since half past nine, and the inverter ran the lights but not the air conditioning, so she worked at the dining table with the balcony door open and the November air coming off the wet road. It was a quarter to one. In nine hours the board of Aripan Systems would convene in Domlur, and the second item on the agenda — after audit — was hers: One Kohbar: programme status and revised recommendation.

Devika had been Vice President, Product, for eighteen months. Aripan built the software on which mid-sized Indian manufacturers ran their distribution — the order a field salesman took from a dealer in Muzaffarpur, the credit limit that dealer held, the schemes the brand ran during Durga Puja, the claims filed afterwards and the credit notes that settled them. Kohbar, the product was called, after the painted wedding chamber of Mithila, a name the founder chose because, he said, everything important in a household got decided in that room.

The recommendation in her deck had changed four times in six days. The version that would go up at ten o'clock said Aripan should collapse its seven forked customer deployments into a single multi-tenant scheme-and-claims engine, beginning with three customers in January and finishing before the Goods and Services Tax changes landed in April. She believed about sixty per cent of that. What she had no confidence about was which of the eleven people whose agreement the plan required would still hold their stated position when the meeting ended — or which of them had told her the truth.

2. Aripan Systems

Rajshekhar Thakur and Farida Qureshi founded Aripan Systems in Ranchi in 2016, above a tyre showroom on Circular Road. Thakur had spent nine years selling enterprise software to cement and fertiliser companies across Bihar and Jharkhand, convinced that a manufacturer's blindness began the moment a truck left the depot. Primary sales — factory to distributor — were instrumented to the rupee. Secondary sales — distributor to the 2.3 lakh small dealers who actually sold to consumers — were a fog of paper order books, WhatsApp photographs and end-of-month reconciliation. Qureshi wrote the first ordering application in eleven weeks.

The company grew the way Indian business-software companies of its generation grew: slowly, on customer money, against spreadsheets. It moved its registered office to Bengaluru in 2019 while keeping a 270-person support centre in Ranchi, the reason it could price a mid-market contract at a third of an SAP implementation. By FY26 Kohbar carried ₹148 crore of annual recurring revenue across 421 customers — 41 of them enterprise accounts contributing seventy-one per cent of that revenue — and Hornbill Growth Partners had put ₹410 crore into the company in 2024 at a valuation of ₹1,900 crore.

Two earlier decisions shaped everything Devika could now propose. The first came in September 2022, when Aripan won Rayyan Nutrition FZE, a Dubai group whose Indian subsidiary made packaged dairy, nutrition powders and infant cereals and sold them through 2,300 distributors into some 380,000 outlets. Rayyan was the logo that made Aripan credible against the category leaders; it had also just been burned by a shared-tenancy vendor. To close it, Thakur agreed to Schedule 4 of the master services agreement: Rayyan India would run on a dedicated deployment, and Aripan would not alter that instance's data schema, scheme-calculation logic or deployment topology without Rayyan's written consent, on forty-five days' notice, with termination for convenience on ninety days if the clause were breached. The contract came up for renewal on 31 March 2027.

The second was the 2023 acquisition of Sohrai Labs, a Kolkata firm of forty engineers whose claims-and-settlement module was better than anything Aripan had built. Aripan paid ₹31 crore, mostly in stock, with an earn-out concluded in March 2026 and retention agreements for the senior Sohrai people running to March 2027. The module was never rewritten into Kohbar's architecture; it was wired alongside it. Six of the seven forks Devika now proposed to collapse existed because the claims engine and the ordering engine had never agreed on what a dealer was.

3. The industry

The Indian market for distribution and field-force software had been, for a decade, a quiet and profitable corner. Bizom and FieldAssist had built substantial businesses in it; the horizontal platforms — Zoho, Freshworks, Salesforce, SAP — circled it without quite fitting the Indian secondary-sales problem, which was less about pipeline management than about schemes, credit and trust between a distributor and a dealer who had known each other twenty years. Aripan's pitch was that it understood that relationship. Its risk was that the relationship was being dismantled.

Quick commerce had changed the arithmetic faster than the category had modelled. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart had pulled a visible share of metro top-up purchasing out of general trade; Reliance Retail and the JioMart network were consolidating the wholesale layer; and the Open Network for Digital Commerce held out the possibility that dealers might one day order from any brand through any buyer application, making the brand's own field application — Kohbar's core — optional. None of this had yet dented Aripan's renewals. All of it appeared in every investor memorandum written about the company.

Regulation bore on the product directly. The GST Council's phased extension of mandatory electronic invoicing had, by 2026, pulled businesses above ₹5 crore of turnover into the e-invoice regime, and a further tightening scheduled for 1 April 2027 would require that credit notes issued against trade schemes be linked, line by line, to the original invoice reference numbers. Kohbar's seven forks calculated schemes seven different ways and issued credit notes through four different code paths. Every one of them would need work before April. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had separately made dealer and field-representative data — names, phone numbers, route-plan location traces — a compliance surface Aripan's consent architecture handled, in Qureshi's phrase, "adequately in five deployments and by assertion in the other two."

Aripan's exposure was not only Indian. Rayyan ran Kohbar in the Emirates and Oman as well as India; a Nairobi agri-inputs group had signed in 2025; and Vikram Sethi, who ran sales from New Jersey, had two North American prospects whose security reviews had flagged the single-tenant architecture as an audit concern.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

One Kohbar was announced internally on 19 January 2026. The belief then, set out in a two-page memo from Thakur, was that unification would take two quarters, cost about ₹14 crore, cut the cost of serving enterprise customers by a quarter, and make the company saleable. Qureshi's estimate, attached, was fourteen weeks with twenty-two engineers.

In April, Anupam Basak's team in Toronto published the analysis that gave the programme its financial spine: a model of "scheme leakage" — claims paid against schemes not in fact earned — putting recoverable leakage across the enterprise base at ₹38 crore a year, of which a unified engine might capture sixty per cent. Stakeholder mapping and management

Who decides, who influences, who blocks — and what each of them actually needs from you.

Section oneA Tuesday in October

On the morning of Tuesday 14 October 2025, Devika Raghunathan opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for three weeks. She is the group product manager for payments and settlements at Makarand Commerce Cloud, a Bengaluru company whose order-management software runs the back office of roughly 1,900 mid-market Indian retail brands — the kind of business that sells on its own website, on Amazon and Flipkart, and through two hundred physical stores, and needs one ledger that reconciles all of it. Makarand bills ₹146 crore a year and employs 420 people. Devika's area accounts for about a third of that revenue.

The decision in front of her was narrow and unglamorous. Makarand's original settlement-reconciliation engine, known internally as Ledger 1, had been written in 2018 and could no longer keep up: during the Diwali week just past, reconciliation for the largest merchants had run eleven hours late on four consecutive days. A replacement, Ledger 2, had been in build for seven months and was working. The question was how to move everyone onto it. Option A was a single cutover on the weekend of 18 January — fast, cheap, and irreversible in practice, because once the new engine started writing settlement records there was no clean way back. Option B was to run both engines in parallel for a quarter, compare their output daily, and switch merchants across in tranches. Option B cost an extra ₹1.1 crore in cloud infrastructure and contract engineering, and it pushed the decommissioning of Ledger 1 — and the ₹40 lakh a quarter it consumed — out to July.

Devika believed Option B was right. She had also, by Tuesday, understood that being right was not the binding constraint. In March of that year a smaller change to settlement timing had been approved by her predecessor, shipped on schedule, and reversed forty-one hours later after the operations head of Makarand's largest customer telephoned Makarand's chief executive directly. Nobody in that sequence had behaved badly. The change had simply been approved by people who were not the people who could stop it. What Devika needed before she wrote a line of her recommendation was an honest answer to four questions: who actually decides this, who influences whoever decides, who can block it after it is decided, and what does each of those people need in order to say yes and stay said.

Section twoThe idea, stated precisely

A stakeholder, in the sense used here, is any person or group who can affect the outcome of a decision or is materially affected by it. That definition — deliberately two-sided — comes from the strategy scholar R. Edward Freeman, whose 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach gave the term its modern currency, though the word had been coined two decades earlier in a 1963 internal memorandum at the Stanford Research Institute, where it was defined as "those groups without whose support the organization would cease to exist." Stakeholder mapping is the practice of enumerating those people for a specific decision, and then classifying them along whatever dimensions determine how you should treat them. Stakeholder management is what you do with the map: allocating your finite attention, and giving each person the particular kind of evidence that would move them.

The problem the idea was invented to solve is the one Devika's predecessor hit. In any organisation larger than about fifteen people, the set of people whose approval is formally required and the set of people who can actually stop a decision have stopped being the same set. Org charts describe reporting; they do not describe influence, and they say nothing at all about customers, regulators or partners, who sit outside the chart entirely and are frequently the most powerful actors in the room. A mapping discipline exists because human intuition about "who matters here" is reliably biased toward people who are physically nearby, who share your function, and who are pleasant to talk to.

The classification most practitioners use is the power–interest grid, set out by the British academic Aubrey Mendelow in 1981 and refined endlessly since. Power is the capacity to stop the decision or unblock it. Interest is how much the outcome changes the person's own week, quarter or number. The two are independent, and that independence is the whole point: high power with low interest is a landmine, because the person is not watching and will not be consulted, but retains the ability to reverse you the moment they notice. A later and more demanding model, from Ronald Mitchell, Bradley Agle and Donna Wood in 1997, adds a third axis — urgency, the degree to which the person's claim is time-sensitive — and argues that people acquire "salience" in a manager's mind in proportion to how many of power, legitimacy and urgency they hold at once.

The sentence Devika could say in a meeting without sounding like a management textbook: "Before we choose the option, let us agree who decides this, who can reverse it, and what each of them would need to see."

Section threeHow it actually works

Practitioners describe the method as four steps. It is really seven, and the three that go unmentioned are where the work is.

Step zero, unwritten: name the decision precisely enough that the list is finite. "Stakeholders of the payments team" is not a list; it is everybody. "People who can affect, or are affected by, the choice between a single cutover on 18 January and a parallel run through March" is a list, and it has a natural boundary. Devika wrote the decision at the top of the page and did not let herself add a name unless she could say, in one clause, how that person touched that choice. The list came to eight. Maps that run to forty names are almost always maps of an area rather than of a decision, and they are unusable because attention cannot be allocated across forty people.

Step one: enumerate by mechanism, not by org chart. Devika walked four paths deliberately: up (who signs off on spend of this size), down and sideways (whose work changes on 19 January), outward (which customers and partners feel it), and backward (who was burnt by the March reversal and will pattern-match). The outward path produced the name that the org chart could never have: Farida Qureshi, the operations head at Phalak Retail Group, Makarand's largest account at ₹6.2 crore of annual contract value, whose quarter-end close depends on settlement files arriving before 06:00.

Step two, unwritten: separate decision rights from influence. These are different questions and blending them is the most common error in the whole practice. Decision rights are a matter of record — who is accountable, who must be consulted, who holds a veto and on what grounds. Influence is a matter of behaviour — whose opinion actually moves the accountable person. Devika drew them as two different pictures, and the gap between the pictures was the interesting part.

Step three: score power and interest, on a scale coarse enough to argue about. One to five on each, with a written justification per score. The justification matters more than the number; a score you cannot defend in a sentence is a guess wearing a uniform.

Step four, unwritten: record the current stance and the required stance separately. Most maps record only how supportive someone is. The useful quantity is the gap — the distance between where the person stands today and where they need to stand for the decision to hold. A champion who is already a champion needs nothing. A powerful sceptic whom you merely need to not veto is a smaller job than a powerful neutral whose active sponsorship you require. The required stance is a choice, and choosing it modestly is how a product manager buys back time.

Step five: write down what each person needs — the specific currency, not "communication." A chief financial officer does not need a demo; he needs a number with a bounded downside. An engineering leader does not need a business case; she needs a rollback plan and an honest defect budget. A support head needs a ticket-volume forecast and the headcount to survive it. A customer needs a named human being and a written commitment.

Step six: allocate attention in proportion to the gap, and re-run the map on a cadence. The map is a derivative of the decision and the calendar; it decays. Devika's rule was to redo it whenever the decision changed shape, whenever the board or the leadership team reset a target, and otherwise monthly.

Read the grid carefully and one feature should nag. Anand Krishnan, the chief risk and compliance officer, sits at power five and interest two. He is not following this project. He will not attend the review. He holds a veto on anything that changes how settlement records are retained, because Makarand's merchants are reconciling money that moves through Unified Payments Interface rails and the audit trail is not negotiable. A team that reads the grid as a to-do list ordered by how much people are talking will speak to Anand last, in December, and discover a constraint that invalidates the January date. The grid's top-left quadrant is not a low-priority zone. It is the zone in which surprises are manufactured.

The gap is salience × (required stance − current stance); where the person is already where they need to be, the gap is zero and they consume no engagement time. Devika had, realistically, twelve hours a week for stakeholder work, and she allocated them in proportion to gap.
