Section fiveSeven things a learner has to get straight

Decision rights and influence are different pictures

Formal authority answers "whose signature is required." Influence answers "whose opinion changes the signer's mind." Confusing them produces the most expensive failure in the practice: a decision that is properly approved and then quietly reversed. In Devika's case the two pictures diverged sharply, and the divergence was the actionable finding.

The required stance is a decision, not an observation

Beginners set every required stance to +2 and then wonder why they have no time. Most stakeholders need only to be neutral. Deciding, explicitly, that Farida needs to reach zero rather than plus two saved Devika roughly two hours a week and, more importantly, changed the content of the conversation: she stopped trying to sell the migration and started negotiating a guarantee.

Power is situational, and the situation is the decision

Ramesh Pillai's power score of 2 is specific to this choice. On a decision about support tooling his power would be 5. Carrying one global "stakeholder map of the company" across decisions is the single most common way the practice degenerates into decoration. Scores are written against a decision or they are meaningless.

Opposition is information before it is an obstacle

Farida's −2 was not irrationality; it encoded a real cost that Makarand's internal plan had not priced. Treating a low stance purely as resistance to be managed is how organisations ship confidently into a wall. The first question on encountering opposition is not "how do I move them" but "what do they know that my plan does not."

The map tells you where to spend attention, not what to say

A high gap score tells Devika that Farida deserves 3.3 hours. It says nothing about whether those hours should be spent on a written service-level commitment, a tranche order that puts Phalak last, or an offer to run Phalak's reconciliation manually for a month. That is judgement, and the map is upstream of it.

What the method cannot tell you

Three things, permanently. It cannot tell you whether the decision itself is correct — a perfectly managed stakeholder map can deliver enthusiastic consensus for a bad migration. It cannot detect stakeholders you failed to name, and the omitted stakeholder is the one that hurts. And it cannot price the cost of the managing itself: attention spent on alignment is attention not spent on the product, and there exists a level of stakeholder management that is indistinguishable from not doing the job.

Questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask first

Before relying on a map, ask: which of these scores would change if I were wrong about one person's incentive? Who is on this list only because they are loud? Who is missing because they are junior, remote, or in another time zone? And — the question that catches the March-2025 failure — if this decision were reversed three weeks after we shipped it, who would most plausibly have caused the reversal, and is that person currently in the bottom band of my chart?

Section sixHow this changes by product type and company stage

In consumer products the users are numerous, anonymous and individually powerless; the substantive stakeholders are almost entirely internal — brand, legal, trust and safety, the app-store relationship — plus, in India, the platform intermediaries and payment rails everybody depends on. Maps are shorter, and the difficult quadrant is high-power, low-interest: a general counsel who learns about a feature from a screenshot. In B2B, which is Makarand's world, individual customers carry real power because revenue is concentrated, and the map crosses the company boundary as a matter of course; the buyer, the user and the person who signs the renewal are frequently three different people with conflicting interests, and mapping inside a single account is a second exercise in its own right. In marketplaces the hardest stakeholders are the two sides themselves, who are structurally in tension — a change that helps demand usually taxes supply — and neither side has a single representative, so the practical move is to identify the small number of large participants who behave as proxies and map them explicitly.

By stage, the difference is real but not the one people expect. In a thirty-person company the map is short and largely unnecessary as a written artefact, because everyone is in the same room; what a founder-led company lacks is not information but the discipline of asking what each person needs, and the characteristic failure is the founder who is simultaneously the decider, the veto and the loudest opinion. In a large company the map is long, the decision rights are documented, and the binding problem shifts to influence: the approvals are obtainable and the reversals are frequent. The middle — roughly Makarand's 420 people — is the hardest, because the org chart has grown past the point where everyone knows everyone, but the decision-rights documents have not yet been written.

Section sevenCommon mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

Mapping the department instead of the decision

Symptom: a map with more than fifteen names that has not been updated in a quarter. Misunderstanding: that stakeholders are an attribute of a team rather than of a choice. Diagnostic: ask the author to say, in one clause each, how the bottom five names touch the decision. If three of the five produce a pause, the map is of an area.

Confusing the loud with the powerful

Symptom: the person who comments most in the review also receives the most one-to-one time. Misunderstanding: volume read as power. Diagnostic: for each person, ask what specifically they could do to stop this — name the mechanism. "They would be unhappy" is not a mechanism.

Managing to agreement rather than to a stance

Symptom: the project has a long alignment phase and a short build phase, and everyone is nominally supportive. Misunderstanding: that consensus is the goal rather than a sufficient stance from each person. Diagnostic: ask what the minimum acceptable position is for each stakeholder; if the answer is "supportive" for all of them, no prioritisation has occurred.

Treating the map as private

Symptom: a scoring spreadsheet nobody outside the PM has seen, often because it would embarrass someone. Misunderstanding: that the map is an assessment of people rather than of a decision. Diagnostic: ask whether the "what they need" column could be shown to the person it describes. If not, it has been written as a judgement rather than as a requirement, and it will age badly.

Section eightWhat good looks like

Handled well, the same decision produces very little drama. The map is one page, written against a named choice, dated, and shared with the engineering lead and the sponsor. It distinguishes four decision rights and names the single accountable person. It records, for each stakeholder, a required stance that is as modest as the situation allows, and a currency — the specific form of evidence that would move them. The high-power, low-interest people are contacted first rather than last, because their constraints are the ones that can invalidate a plan. The customer with the largest gap is engaged directly by the product manager, not through an account manager relaying summaries. And when an external event changes a score, the map is re-run within a week and the reallocation is visible, so that nobody has to guess why the product manager's calendar suddenly changed shape.

Section nineWhat Devika decided

On 11 November, Devika recommended a modified Option B and the recommendation held. The parallel run was shortened from a quarter to seven weeks, cutting the incremental cost from ₹1.1 crore to ₹62 lakh — a number built specifically for Suresh Iyer, with a stated worst case of ₹78 lakh if the comparison surfaced defects requiring an eighth and ninth week. Phalak Retail Group was moved to the last migration tranche, in March, with a written commitment on the 06:00 settlement file and Devika's own mobile number as the escalation path; Farida Qureshi moved from −2 to 0 and did not need to be persuaded of anything further. Anand Krishnan was consulted on 20 October, eight weeks earlier than the previous project had consulted him, and surfaced a record-retention requirement that added four days of work and would have added five weeks if found in January.

The reasoning underneath all of it was a single reframing. Devika stopped treating the migration as a technical decision requiring approvals and started treating it as a set of eight distinct commitments, each owed to a different person, each with its own currency and its own minimum acceptable position. The engineering plan barely changed. The probability that the plan survived contact with the organisation changed a great deal.

What to learn next, and why. Decision records and DACI/RACI turn the informal decision-rights picture in Figure 3 into an artefact the organisation can hold itself to, which is what prevents the March reversal from recurring. Prioritising under constraints is the natural sequel, because a stakeholder map produces a set of competing legitimate claims and something has to adjudicate between them. Influence without authority supplies the behaviour the map only points at: the map says Farida needs 3.3 hours, and that topic addresses what happens inside them.
